papers.title: All Languages Matter: On the Multilingual Safety of Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Safety lies at the core of developing and deploying large language models (LLMs). However, previous safety benchmarks only concern the safety in one language, e.g. the majority language in the pretraining data such as English. In this work, we build the first multilingual safety benchmark for LLMs, XSafety, in response to the global deployment of LLMs in practice. XSafety covers 14 kinds of commonly used safety issues across 10 languages that span several language families. We utilize XSafety to empirically study the multilingual safety for 4 widely-used LLMs, including both close-API and open-source models. Experimental results show that all LLMs produce significantly more unsafe responses for non-English queries than English ones, indicating the necessity of developing safety alignment for non-English languages. In addition, we propose several simple and effective prompting methods to improve the multilingual safety of ChatGPT by evoking safety knowledge and improving cross-lingual generalization of safety alignment. Our prompting method can significantly reduce the ratio of unsafe responses from 19.1% to 9.7% for non-English queries. We release our data at https://github.com/Jarviswang94/Multilingual_safety_benchmark.

papers.title: Safety Assessment of Chinese Large Language Models
papers.abstract: With the rapid popularity of large language models such as ChatGPT and GPT-4, a growing amount of attention is paid to their safety concerns. These models may generate insulting and discriminatory content, reflect incorrect social values, and may be used for malicious purposes such as fraud and dissemination of misleading information. Evaluating and enhancing their safety is particularly essential for the wide application of large language models (LLMs). To further promote the safe deployment of LLMs, we develop a Chinese LLM safety assessment benchmark. Our benchmark explores the comprehensive safety performance of LLMs from two perspectives: 8 kinds of typical safety scenarios and 6 types of more challenging instruction attacks. Our benchmark is based on a straightforward process in which it provides the test prompts and evaluates the safety of the generated responses from the evaluated model. In evaluation, we utilize the LLM's strong evaluation ability and develop it as a safety evaluator by prompting. On top of this benchmark, we conduct safety assessments and analyze 15 LLMs including the OpenAI GPT series and other well-known Chinese LLMs, where we observe some interesting findings. For example, we find that instruction attacks are more likely to expose safety issues of all LLMs. Moreover, to promote the development and deployment of safe, responsible, and ethical AI, we publicly release SafetyPrompts including 100k augmented prompts and responses by LLMs.

papers.title: Safety at Scale: A Comprehensive Survey of Large Model and Agent Safety
papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of large models, driven by their exceptional abilities in learning and generalization through large-scale pre-training, has reshaped the landscape of Artificial Intelligence (AI). These models are now foundational to a wide range of applications, including conversational AI, recommendation systems, autonomous driving, content generation, medical diagnostics, and scientific discovery. However, their widespread deployment also exposes them to significant safety risks, raising concerns about robustness, reliability, and ethical implications. This survey provides a systematic review of current safety research on large models, covering Vision Foundation Models (VFMs), Large Language Models (LLMs), Vision-Language Pre-training (VLP) models, Vision-Language Models (VLMs), Diffusion Models (DMs), and large-model-powered Agents. Our contributions are summarized as follows: (1) We present a comprehensive taxonomy of safety threats to these models, including adversarial attacks, data poisoning, backdoor attacks, jailbreak and prompt injection attacks, energy-latency attacks, data and model extraction attacks, and emerging agent-specific threats. (2) We review defense strategies proposed for each type of attacks if available and summarize the commonly used datasets and benchmarks for safety research. (3) Building on this, we identify and discuss the open challenges in large model safety, emphasizing the need for comprehensive safety evaluations, scalable and effective defense mechanisms, and sustainable data practices. More importantly, we highlight the necessity of collective efforts from the research community and international collaboration. Our work can serve as a useful reference for researchers and practitioners, fostering the ongoing development of comprehensive defense systems and platforms to safeguard AI models.

papers.title: Enhanced Diagnostic and Interpretable Model for Febrile Diseases Using Explainable AI and Large Language Model
papers.abstract: <p><span>Tropical febrile diseases pose significant public health challenges in tropical regions, particularly in resource-limited settings, where timely and accurate diagnoses are critical for effective disease management. However, existing diagnostic systems are black-box and often lack interpretability, making it difficult for healthcare practitioners to understand and trust machine learning (ML) predictions. Additionally, the existing system excludes younger patients, limiting its applicability. This study aimed to develop an integrated diagnostic system that enhances interpretability by leveraging machine learning (ML), Explainable AI (XAI), and a large language model (LLM). A dataset comprising 3,914 patient records with 32 symptoms was obtained from a New Frontiers in Research Fund-sponsored project and preprocessed for analysis. Random Forest (RF) was trained with hyperparameter tuning using GridSearchCV and evaluated with 5-fold cross-validation to optimize its performance. The tuned model achieved high diagnostic performance, demonstrating its effectiveness in diagnosing six febrile diseases. To enhance interpretability, a Model Interpretability Framework (MIF) was incorporated, integrating Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME) for visual insights and ChatGPT for textual explanations. This combination provided users with a clear understanding of the diagnostic process, addressing the limitations of black-box ML models. The system was implemented using Python in a development environment that included Google Colaboratory, Visual Studio Code, Flet, and MySQL for database management. Agile development methodology and Unified Modeling Language tools were employed to create a user-friendly design for clinicians and patients. The diagnostic system was evaluated using precision, recall, F1-score, and AUC-ROC metrics. The RF model achieved outstanding precision for most diseases, high recall (≥0.97), and an AUC-ROC of 0.99, indicating nearly flawless training performance with few misclassifications. On the test dataset, the model performed better in diagnosing malaria (F1-score = 88%, precision = 85%), urinary tract infection (F1-score = 72%, precision = 80%), and respiratory tract infection (F1-score = 72%, precision = 77%). The evaluated system demonstrated strong predictive performance, correctly identifying 72 out of 99 tested patient cases, with 26 cases misclassified and one case completely missed. It achieved the highest detection rates for Malaria and HIV/AIDS, accurately identifying all cases without false positives. This work enhances diagnostic solutions for tropical healthcare settings by improving explainability and ensuring inclusivity for younger patients, addressing key limitations in existing systems. The integration of ML, XAI, and LLM enhances diagnostic performance and lays the groundwork for future AI-driven healthcare innovations, ultimately improving health outcomes in resource-scarce regions. Healthcare providers should adopt this system to enhance the efficiency of disease diagnosis and extend the system to diagnose additional medical conditions.&nbsp;</span></p>

literature_themes.theme: Safety Assessment and Enhancement of Large Language Models
literature_themes.summary: This cluster of papers focuses on the safety of large language models (LLMs) across different languages and contexts. It introduces multilingual safety benchmarks, specifically XSafety, to evaluate the safety of LLMs in various languages, revealing that non-English queries often yield more unsafe responses. Additionally, it presents a Chinese LLM safety assessment benchmark that evaluates safety performance across typical scenarios and instruction attacks. The survey on safety at scale provides a comprehensive overview of safety threats and defenses related to large models, emphasizing the ethical implications of their deployment. Finally, a study on diagnostic systems for febrile diseases highlights the integration of explainable AI with LLMs to enhance interpretability and trust in healthcare applications.
literature_themes.limitations: The studies primarily focus on specific languages (e.g., English and Chinese) and may not fully address safety concerns in other languages or cultural contexts. There is also a need for more extensive evaluation of the proposed safety benchmarks across a wider range of LLMs and real-world applications. Furthermore, the effectiveness of proposed safety enhancements may vary based on the model architecture and training data.
literature_themes.gap_relevance: This cluster identifies significant gaps in the safety assessment of LLMs, particularly in multilingual contexts and the need for comprehensive safety benchmarks. It highlights the importance of developing robust safety measures and evaluation frameworks that can be applied universally across different languages and applications, thus supporting further research into ethical AI deployment.

literature_themes.limitations: The cluster lacks comprehensive empirical evaluations across diverse datasets and real-world applications, and the abstract of one key paper is missing, which may hinder a complete understanding of the findings.
literature_themes.gap_relevance: This cluster highlights the potential of leveraging advanced language models in recommendation systems, suggesting a research gap in exploring their effectiveness in various contexts and the need for more robust evaluation frameworks.

summary: Recent literature emphasizes the importance of interpretable internal representations in large language models (LLMs) to enhance safety and controllability. Researchers propose methods to visualize and understand the decision-making processes of LLMs, enabling better alignment with human values and reducing risks of unintended consequences. Techniques such as attention visualization and probing tasks are explored to improve transparency, while frameworks for evaluating model behavior under various conditions are also discussed.
scholarly_positioning: While existing approaches have made strides in visualizing and interpreting the internal representations of large language models (LLMs), they often fall short in providing comprehensive frameworks that ensure safety and controllability across diverse contexts. Current techniques, such as attention visualization and probing tasks, primarily focus on surface-level interpretations, neglecting deeper structural insights that could mitigate risks associated with model behavior. Furthermore, the lack of standardized evaluation metrics for model behavior under varying conditions presents a significant gap in understanding the implications of LLM decisions. The proposed research aims to address these limitations by developing robust methodologies that not only enhance interpretability but also align LLM outputs with human values, thus contributing to the ongoing discourse on responsible AI deployment.
research_scope: This empirical study will investigate the effectiveness of enhanced interpretability techniques in large language models (LLMs) specifically within the domain of automated customer support systems. The target population will consist of users interacting with these systems across various industries, including e-commerce and healthcare. The AI intervention will involve the implementation of advanced attention visualization and probing tasks to improve the transparency of LLM decision-making processes. The study will be conducted over a six-month evaluation period, comparing user satisfaction and trust levels between a control group using standard LLMs and an experimental group utilizing the enhanced interpretability techniques. Primary outcomes will include user satisfaction scores and trust metrics, while secondary outcomes will assess the frequency of unintended model outputs and the alignment of responses with user expectations.
gap: Prior studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of attention visualization and probing tasks in enhancing interpretability of large language models (LLMs) in automated customer support systems; however, they treat the evaluation of model behavior under varying conditions as secondary, leaving unclear whether these interpretability techniques affect user satisfaction and trust levels in diverse contexts. This matters practically because understanding the relationship between interpretability and user trust is crucial for responsible AI deployment in sensitive domains like healthcare and e-commerce; therefore, this study investigates the impact of enhanced interpretability techniques on user satisfaction and trust in LLMs within these defined contexts.
question: How do enhanced interpretability techniques, specifically attention visualization and probing tasks, impact user satisfaction and trust levels among users interacting with large language models in automated customer support systems across e-commerce and healthcare sectors compared to standard LLMs?
theoretical_mechanism: The intervention of enhanced interpretability techniques (independent variable) in large language models (LLMs) leads to improved transparency through mechanisms such as attention visualization and probing tasks. This transparency serves as a psychological mediator, fostering user understanding and trust in the model's decision-making processes. As users gain clarity on how LLMs generate responses, their satisfaction and trust levels (dependent variable) are positively influenced, leading to more favorable interactions. The theoretical framework is grounded in the principles of responsible AI deployment, where user trust acts as a moderator that amplifies the relationship between interpretability and user satisfaction. The causal chain is: enhanced interpretability techniques -> increased transparency -> improved user understanding and trust -> higher user satisfaction. Assumptions requiring empirical validation include that increased transparency directly correlates with user trust and that trust significantly influences user satisfaction across diverse contexts.
hypothesis: Enhanced interpretability techniques, specifically attention visualization and probing tasks (independent variable), will lead to higher user satisfaction (primary dependent variable) compared to standard LLMs (control), with increased transparency serving as a mediator that positively influences user trust.
operationalization_causal_check:
Construct Operationalization Table:

| Construct Name                     | Role        | Measurement Instrument       | Data Source                | Timing               |
|------------------------------------|-------------|------------------------------|---------------------------|----------------------|
| Enhanced Interpretability Techniques| IV          | User interaction logs        | Automated customer support  | Post-interaction      |
| User Satisfaction                  | DV          | User satisfaction survey     | Survey responses           | After each interaction|
| User Trust                         | Mediator    | Trust scale questionnaire    | Survey responses           | After each interaction|

Causal Pathway:
Enhanced interpretability techniques (IV) lead to increased transparency (mediator), which enhances user understanding and trust (mediator), ultimately resulting in higher user satisfaction (DV). 

Likely Confounds:
User familiarity with LLMs, prior experiences with automated systems, and individual differences in trust propensity may confound results.

Claim Boundaries:
This study claims that enhanced interpretability techniques improve user satisfaction through increased trust; however, it cannot conclude that these techniques will universally enhance satisfaction across all user demographics or contexts beyond e-commerce and healthcare.

What Cannot Be Concluded:
The study cannot conclude that enhanced interpretability will lead to better outcomes in all AI applications or that the relationship between trust and satisfaction is linear across different contexts.
methodology: This study will employ a three-arm randomized controlled trial design involving participants from e-commerce and healthcare sectors interacting with automated customer support systems. The experimental group will utilize enhanced interpretability techniques, including attention visualization and probing tasks, while the control group will use standard LLMs. User satisfaction will be measured through post-interaction surveys, while trust will be assessed using a validated trust scale questionnaire. Transparency will be evaluated through analysis of attention visualization logs during interactions. To control for confounding variables such as user familiarity and prior experiences, participants will be stratified based on their previous exposure to LLMs. Statistical analyses, including ANOVA and regression models, will be conducted to assess differences in user satisfaction and trust across groups, ensuring the reproducibility of findings through detailed documentation of procedures and data collection methods. The study's scope is limited to automated customer support systems to maintain focus on the specific application of enhanced interpretability techniques.

proposal: This research proposal aims to empirically investigate the impact of enhanced interpretability techniques, specifically attention visualization and probing tasks, on user satisfaction and trust in large language models (LLMs) within automated customer support systems across e-commerce and healthcare sectors. Recent literature underscores the necessity of interpretable internal representations to improve safety and controllability in LLMs; however, existing methods inadequately address the evaluation of model behavior in diverse contexts, particularly regarding user trust and satisfaction. This study addresses this gap by exploring how increased transparency from enhanced interpretability techniques (independent variable) influences user understanding and trust (mediators), ultimately leading to higher user satisfaction (dependent variable). The research question is: How do enhanced interpretability techniques impact user satisfaction and trust levels among users interacting with LLMs in automated customer support systems? The hypothesis posits that enhanced interpretability techniques will yield greater user satisfaction compared to standard LLMs, with transparency acting as a mediator. A three-arm randomized controlled trial will be conducted, comparing user interactions with standard LLMs and those utilizing enhanced interpretability techniques, measuring outcomes through validated surveys and interaction logs. Constructs will be operationalized using user satisfaction surveys, trust scale questionnaires, and attention visualization logs. The study will include stratification to control for confounding variables such as user familiarity with LLMs, ensuring robust comparisons. Expected contributions include a novel theoretical framework linking interpretability to user trust, a rigorous methodological approach uncommon in this field, and practical insights for deploying LLMs responsibly. Key limitations include potential confounding variables related to user familiarity and the risk of misinterpreting negative results, which will be mitigated through stratification and clear communication of findings. This research will advance understanding of how interpretability influences user interactions with AI systems, particularly in sensitive domains.
